title: Triage queue with a hard capacity cap
problem: Without a hard limit on concurrent work, a side-practice consultant accepts every engagement that looks 'doable' and ends up with too many clients at once eating evenings and weekends — and family-first, the value the whole practice is built to protect, quietly falsifies. This feature makes the load-bearing rule structural rather than aspirational: at most two active builds running at a time. The triage queue is intentionally uncapped — the scarce resource is a build slot, not a spot in line — so a submission made while both slots are full becomes a real queued proposal rather than a dropped one. The homepage shows the current state so a visitor knows immediately whether a build slot is open, and the server refuses to promote an engagement to active past the cap. The public waitlist is not a flaw to hide — scarcity reads as seriousness. The active cap is the single rule of the portal that does not bend at runtime; moving it is a reviewed code change, never a toggle.
analysis: The cap is enforced where it cannot be wished away — in the server, folded into the UPDATE that promotes a session to active so two concurrent promotions can't both win. The current load is not a number someone maintains by hand; it is counted directly from the engagement records, so it is always true and it decrements on its own when a build ships. A public endpoint reports whether the practice is at the active cap, and the homepage hero turns that into a plain-language indicator of how many build slots are open. Triage is uncapped: a visitor submitting while both build slots are full still gets a real queued session, and the at-capacity state only changes the copy they see (you are in the queue, I start when a build frees up) — nothing is dropped. There is still no runtime override: no admin toggle raises the cap, because the rule that must not bend should not have a soft switch in the code. The number lives in a single named constant (ACTIVE_CAP) so raising it is a deliberate, reviewable change.

decisions.decision: Hard cap of one active build plus one in triage, with no exception path
decisions.rationale: This is the bedrock defence. If it breaks, family-first collapses — three concurrent clients against side-practice hours consumes weekends. The failure pattern it structurally prevents is the optimism of 'I can squeeze this one in'.
decisions.recommendation: Enforce it server-side, not as a soft warning, and provide no override anywhere in the admin surface.

decisions.decision: Cap raised to two active builds; the triage queue is uncapped
decisions.rationale: A deliberate revision of the original 1+1 rule. Two concurrent builds is still small enough to protect family time at side-practice hours, but doubles throughput when both projects have natural wait states (waiting on a client reply, a deploy, a payment). Capping triage turned out to do harm rather than good: it dropped real proposals on the floor at the moment of intake. Decoupling the two — cap the scarce resource (a build slot), let the queue grow — keeps the family-first guarantee intact while never losing an inbound lead. The 'no soft switch' doctrine is preserved: this change moved a constant in a reviewed commit, not a runtime toggle.
decisions.recommendation: Keep the active cap in the single ACTIVE_CAP constant; report triageCap as null from /api/capacity to mean uncapped; never re-introduce a triage cap or an admin override without an equally deliberate decision.

decisions.decision: The public capacity indicator is an asset, not a bug to hide
decisions.rationale: Scarcity adds credibility. A visible 'currently full, waitlist open' positions the consultant as serious rather than unavailable, and the waitlist itself becomes acquisition infrastructure.
decisions.recommendation: Keep the indicator on the homepage hero and let it read straight from real engagement counts so it is never stale.

decisions.decision: Current load is derived from engagement records, never hand-maintained
decisions.rationale: A hand-edited capacity figure drifts the moment someone forgets to update it after an engagement ships. Counting active and triage engagements directly makes the figure self-correcting and removes a standing source of error.
decisions.recommendation: Keep the cap thresholds as named constants next to the counting logic so raising them is a deliberate, reviewable code change.

implementation: The capacity primitive is server-side. functions/api/capacity.ts answers GET /api/capacity with the live active and triage counts, activeCap (the ACTIVE_CAP constant), triageCap (null, meaning uncapped), and an atCap flag that reflects the active cap only. The counting and the single cap constant (ACTIVE_CAP = 2) live in functions/_lib/sessions.ts and are derived from the engagement records in the database. The cap is enforced at promotion time: PATCH /api/sessions/:id { status: 'active' } folds the active count into the UPDATE's WHERE subselect, so a promotion that would push past two matches zero rows and returns 409 — and two concurrent promotions into the last slot can't both win (AUDIT P1.7). Triage is uncapped, so POST /api/sessions never refuses an intake for capacity; a submission made while both slots are full creates a real queued session. On the client side, the homepage hero (src/components/Hero.tsx) fetches /api/capacity on mount and shows how many build slots are open, or 'full, waitlist open'; the footer studio sign and the intake form read the same endpoint. There is deliberately no admin endpoint or toggle that raises the cap.
successCriteria:
- The active-build cap (2) is enforced by the server atomically, not by policy or a soft warning
- Promoting a third session to active is rejected with 409; two concurrent promotions into the last slot yield exactly one winner
- Triage is uncapped: submitting an intake while both slots are full creates a real queued session and is never dropped
- The homepage shows how many build slots are open, read from real engagement counts
- The current load decrements on its own when a build ships — nobody maintains it by hand
- There is no runtime override path anywhere that can raise the cap; moving it is a code change to ACTIVE_CAP
- Reusable as a pattern for any solo-operator service that wants the same structural rule
userGuide: The capacity state is computed automatically from engagement records — there is nothing to update by hand. GET /api/capacity returns the current counts, activeCap, triageCap (null = uncapped), and the atCap flag; the homepage hero, the footer studio sign, and the intake form all read it. The two-active-build limit is enforced atomically inside PATCH /api/sessions/:id when a session is promoted to active. Triage is uncapped, so intake submissions are always accepted into the queue. To change the cap, edit the ACTIVE_CAP constant in functions/_lib/sessions.ts — a deliberate code change, by design, with no UI shortcut.
knownLimitations: The capacity figure reflects engagement records only — it does not model a richer queue with per-slot start dates
The homepage indicator is fetched on page load, so a visitor with a stale tab sees the state from when they opened it until the next load

The queue has no visible position number — a waitlisted visitor sees 'in the queue' but not 'you are 3rd', and with triage now uncapped that queue can grow without an operator-facing depth alert beyond the admin capacity panel's raw count

statusHistory.reason: Capacity gating live; homepage hero shows the slot state and the intake submit path respects the cap.

Code-first verification — feature.json co-located at functions/api/capacity.feature.json. Capacity is now derived live from engagement records via the server; the earlier hand-edited JSON file is gone.

Requirements change: Marc raised his core 'one active project' principle to two. Reopened to revise the load-bearing rule — ACTIVE_CAP 1→2 and the triage cap dropped — across server, client, copy, and tests.

Cap raise shipped end-to-end: ACTIVE_CAP=2, triage uncapped (triageCap reported null), atomic active guard rewired off the constant, intake no longer capacity-rejected, FR/EN copy + hero slot count + admin panel + OG cards + e2e/unit tests all updated to match.

revisions.reason: Code-first overhaul: capacity is now a server endpoint that counts real engagement records, so the feature.json is co-located at functions/api/capacity.feature.json and anchored on capacity.ts. Dropped every stale limitation — the hand-edited file, the manual decrement, the unwired waitlist, and the rebuild-to-update lag are all gone.

revisions.author: marc+claude
revisions.reason: Deliberate decision change: active cap raised 1→2 and the triage cap dropped (queue is now uncapped). The atomic guard now reads ACTIVE_CAP instead of a hardcoded literal and applies to active-only; POST /api/sessions no longer capacity-rejects; /api/capacity reports triageCap null. Carried through FR/EN copy (intake waitlist + hero open-slot count), the admin capacity panel, the OG cards, and the unit/e2e suites. The 'no runtime toggle' doctrine is preserved.
